doc.title: Peter Ecklund interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Choosing repertory for a set with many horns, and Marty Grosz
summary: Many horn players limit the tunes that harmonize well and force long solo-filled tunes; Ecklund credits Marty Grosz for trying to make interesting music.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I had to laugh when Marty was talking about — you know he was actually rehearsing you guys on stage, or handing out instant arrangements. He says I’ll do this and you guys mutter behind him. Now when you set up your set, is it getting increasingly hard as the weeks, not as the weeks, as the days go by at these festivals, to set up, if you’re the leader to do a set, because now you’re thinking well gee those guys did that yesterday? Does it cut down on your repertory choices?

It should. In fact, I don’t hear every set so I might play something tonight that’s already been played. The problem with this particular event is that there are so many horn players. There are not that many tunes, as you know, that can fall into harmonies easily that sound good with harmonizing the lead like that. I mean if we tried to play “Deep © Fiillius Jazz Archive -10-

Purple” with four horns or something, we’d be in big trouble. And that really limits the repertory and also you have to give everybody solos, because that’s why they’re here, so it tends to make the tunes too long. And it’s really kind of difficult to make consistently interesting music. Marty I think is one of the best at that. I mean at least he really makes an effort.
He’s certainly got a sense of humor too.
